strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning four diverse datasets (indoor/outdoor, handheld/drone/robot) against 13 baselines including classical VIO, learning-based VO, visual Gaussian Splatting SLAM, and visual-inertial systems, providing a thorough and convincing comparison landscape.

Strong and consistent quantitative improvements in tracking accuracy (ATE RMSE) and rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) across nearly all tested sequences, with results reported both with and without final global BA/color refinement for fair 'online' comparison.

Well-designed robustness experiments (strided frame-dropping evaluation and a self-captured extreme-condition sequence) that directly and convincingly validate the paper's central claim that IMU fusion improves resilience to degraded visual conditions, which purely visual 3DGS baselines clearly fail under.

Systematic ablation studies isolating the contribution of IMU fusion, loop closure, keyframe initialization strategy, and the loop-closure Gaussian update, each showing meaningful degradation when removed.

Detailed engineering contributions (staged IMU initialization, time-varying bias modeling with temporal smoothness term, PGBA-based loop closure with efficient batched Gaussian pose/scale propagation) are clearly described with sufficient mathematical detail and implementation specifics (thresholds, hyperparameters) in the supplementary to aid reproducibility.
Extensive supplementary material with per-sequence breakdowns, runtime analysis, and dataset statistics enhances transparency and evidentiary support for the claims.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is primarily integrative rather than fundamental: the visual front-end is directly inherited from DROID-SLAM, the inertial residual formulation closely follows standard IMU-preintegration approaches (e.g., ORB-SLAM3/VI-DSO style), and the loop-closure PGBA is adapted from HI-SLAM2; the main contribution is the careful combination and staged optimization of these known components rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Despite being framed as a 'real-time' system, reported frame rates (4-16 FPS with mapping) are slower than the purely-visual HI-SLAM2 baseline, and the authors acknowledge the IMU code is not yet CUDA-optimized, undermining the real-time claim in its current form.

Comparison with the most directly relevant prior work (VINGS-Mono, a visual-inertial 3DGS SLAM system) is largely deferred to related-work discussion rather than included in the main experimental tables; MM3DGS-SLAM results are copied from its paper rather than reproduced under the same protocol, limiting the fairness/completeness of head-to-head comparison with the closest competitors.

The 'extreme conditions' robustness claim rests on a single self-captured sequence with pseudo ground truth from another SLAM system (FAST-LIVO2), which is a relatively weak and potentially circular form of validation given limited sample size.

No code release is confirmed at submission time (project page mentioned but link omitted), and given the system's complexity (multi-stage initialization, joint BA, PGBA, Gaussian update propagation), independent reproducibility without released code would be challenging.

Some robustness/ATE metrics under strided evaluation show known pitfalls (e.g., low ATE with very low recall for baselines), which the paper appropriately discusses, but this also highlights that ATE alone is an imperfect metric throughout the rest of the paper's main tables where only ATE is reported.
